title: Backstage: software catalog and templates
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: The catalog models components such as services and libraries, systems that group them, APIs they provide or consume, resources such as databases and the owners of each.
Each repository holds a `catalog-info.yaml` that describes the component.
A software template asks a few questions, then creates a repository, a pipeline, a deployment configuration and a catalog entry in one run.
Plugins add views for CI results, Kubernetes status, cost or on call.
Backstage is a framework you build and run, not a product you install.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: A catalog full of unowned services
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
During an outage nobody could find who owned the failing service in the portal.
An operator runs a command such as: yq '.spec.owner' catalog-info.yaml
Teams had been reorganised and ownership in many files pointed to groups that no longer existed, so the page for the failing service listed nobody.
The platform team added a check that every entity owner resolves to a real group, a weekly report of orphaned services and a rule that reorganisations update ownership files.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Entities with no valid owner.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: Crossplane: compositions and self service infrastructure
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: A provider is a controller that manages resources in an external system, such as AWS, Azure or Kubernetes.
A composite resource definition declares a new API with a schema, for example a PostgreSQLInstance with size and region fields.
Developers create a claim in their namespace.
Controllers keep reconciling, so manual changes in the cloud console are reverted or reported.
Pin provider versions, test compositions with sample claims and render them before release, monitor reconcile errors and API rate limits, and limit what the provider credentials can do.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: A deleted claim that removed a production database
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
A developer deleted a namespace and the database behind the claim was deleted with it.
An operator runs a command such as: kubectl get postgresqlinstance orders-db -n shop -o jsonpath="{.spec.deletionPolicy}"
The composition used the default Delete policy and had no backup or protection.
When the namespace was removed, the claim, the composite resource and the cloud database all went with it.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Default deletion policy for production data.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: Argo CD ApplicationSets and fleet delivery
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: A central Argo CD instance, or a few of them, manages applications in many target clusters registered as destinations.
An ApplicationSet uses a template and generators to create applications.
Sync waves order resources inside an application, for example namespaces and CRDs before the workloads that use them.
Do not push a change to every cluster at once.
Give teams access to their own projects and destinations through AppProjects and RBAC, and restrict which repositories and clusters each project can use.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: A bad change that reached every cluster in minutes
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
A broken ingress setting was merged and an ApplicationSet synced it to forty clusters at once.
An operator runs a command such as: argocd app list -o name | wc -l
The ApplicationSet used a cluster generator for all production clusters with automated sync, so one merge changed everything at once.
The team added rollout rings by cluster label, a canary ring with health gates, manual approval for the final ring, and an automatic pause when applications became degraded.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Syncing every cluster at once.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: Cluster API and fleet lifecycle
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: A management cluster runs the Cluster API controllers.
A Cluster object points to a control plane object and an infrastructure object.
To upgrade, change the Kubernetes version on the control plane object, wait for it to roll, then update the machine deployments.
A ClusterClass defines a reusable cluster shape with variables.
Plan backups of the management cluster, certificate renewal, node health checks with automatic remediation and a runbook for replacing a failed control plane member.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: An upgrade that stalled halfway
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
A control plane upgrade stopped after the first machine and left the cluster mixed.
An operator runs a command such as: kubectl get machines -n fleet -l cluster.x-k8s.io/cluster-name=prod-eu
The new machine could not start because the machine image for the new version was not available in the region, so the rollout waited.
The team found the image error in the machine conditions, published the image, and added a pre upgrade check that confirms images and quotas exist in every region before a rollout.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: A management cluster with no backup.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: Ephemeral environments and preview deployments
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: A shared staging environment causes conflicts, stale data and waiting.
A namespace per environment is cheap, but cluster wide resources and CRDs are shared.
Environments need realistic data without real customer data.
Set time to live on every environment, scale to zero when idle, apply resource quotas and use cheap node pools.
Post the URL, status and logs link as a comment on the pull request.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: A preview bill that grew every week
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
Preview environments from closed pull requests were never deleted and quietly used nodes.
An operator runs a command such as: kubectl get ns -l type=preview --no-headers | wc -l
The cleanup step ran only when a pull request merged, so abandoned and closed pull requests left their environments behind.
The team added a time to live label, a reaper job that deletes environments older than three days or without an open pull request, and quotas per team with a weekly cost report.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: No time to live on environments.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: Measuring platforms: DORA and developer experience
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: Deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore service measure delivery performance.
Quantitative data misses friction.
Measure how many services use each golden path, the time from a new engineer start to first production deploy, and the time to create a new service.
Track platform availability and incident counts, the support load in tickets and chat, and the share of engineering time spent on repetitive operational work.
Any metric used as a target will be gamed.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: A metric that rose while the work got worse
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
Deployment frequency was used as a target and teams split changes into tiny deploys.
An operator runs a command such as: psql -h metrics -c "select team, count(*) as deploys, avg(lines_changed) as avg_lines from deploys where month
When managers ranked teams by deployment frequency, one team deployed trivial changes to raise the count while lead time and failures did not improve.
The platform team stopped ranking, reported the four measures together as trends, added the survey results and used them to choose the next improvement.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Using DORA as a team ranking.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.
